profile.campus: Westover Hills, San Antonio, Bexar County, Texas (Microsoft's original 2015 San Antonio data center campus)
profile.address: Westover Link, Westover Hills, San Antonio, Bexar County, Texas, 78251
profile.reading:
This building sits on Westover Link in San Antonio's Westover Hills area, the district where Microsoft opened its first two San Antonio data centers in 2015 at roughly $90 million each. That original investment grew into a much larger regional footprint: Silicon Hills News and the San Antonio Report both documented Microsoft's continued expansion in Westover Hills and beyond, and by August 2023 the company operated at least eight data centers across Bexar and Medina counties with cumulative investment exceeding $1.2 billion. San Antonio's city council approved a 15-year Chapter 380 tax reimbursement in 2013 covering 40% of property taxes in exchange for a $250 million Microsoft investment commitment and the creation of 20 high-paying jobs, an incentive package the company has since built well beyond. Named Westover Hills-area buildings identified in local reporting include SAT14 on nearby Wiseman Boulevard, a 411,000-square-foot complex Microsoft has continued expanding through 2024. Construction phases at Microsoft's San Antonio campuses have typically employed several hundred workers, while completed data center buildings tend to run with a comparatively small operating staff of roughly 50 employees once online. Microsoft has not published this specific Westover Link building's square footage or MW capacity, so this registry records the SAT14 figure as regional context rather than a confirmed fact for this exact structure.

CPS Energy, San Antonio's municipally owned electric and gas utility, the largest such public utility in the country, supplies power to Microsoft's San Antonio-area campuses and has cited large commercial and industrial customers, data centers among them, in its own integrated resource planning as it weighs new generation to meet growing demand. Because CPS Energy is municipally owned rather than investor-owned, large-load agreements with customers like Microsoft are negotiated directly with the city-owned utility rather than through the Public Utility Commission of Texas process that governs most of the state's investor-owned utilities.

reading.body:
Microsoft does not publish power consumption, square footage, or capacity at the individual campus level. This facility in Westover Hills is part of a multi-county data center presence in the San Antonio region that has been expanding, but no figures exist in public sources to establish its scale relative to other campuses or to Texas infrastructure.

Texas has 133 mapped data center facilities, of which 18 have published power figures totaling 468 megawatts. This campus cannot be ranked among them because Microsoft discloses only aggregate worldwide statistics: 40+ gigawatts of renewable energy contracted across 500+ data centers in 80+ regions globally. The operator's policy of withholding individual campus specifications means its capacity cannot be compared to the published Texas baseline.

Without disclosed megawatts, the relevance of this campus to AI scaling cannot be assessed from power supply data. Whether it matters depends on information Microsoft has chosen not to publish: the kilowatts dedicated to compute, the timing of capacity additions, and the grid's headroom in Bexar and Medina counties during expansion. These facts are not public.
